Sanquhar
SANG-kur
n. (the Nithsdale burgh at whose cross Richard Cameron and twenty men posted the declaration disowning Charles II on 22 June 1680)
Gaelic sean cathair, the old fort, from sean, old, and cathair, a fort or stronghold.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Sanquhar is the small burgh of upper Nithsdale in Dumfriesshire, on the road between Ayrshire and Dumfries, with a castle of the Crichtons above it and the oldest working post office in Britain. Its day is the twenty-second of June 1680. Richard Cameron, a field preacher who had been ordained in Holland, rode into the burgh with his brother Michael, Michael Cargill and about twenty armed men, drew up at the market cross, sang a psalm, prayed, and read and affixed a declaration which disowned Charles Stuart as king on the ground that he had broken his covenant engagements, usurped the headship of Christ's church and shed the blood of the saints, and declared war against him and all who adhered to him. A reward was set on Cameron's head; he was killed at Airds Moss on the twenty-second of July, a month later, and his head and hands were carried to Edinburgh. Cargill excommunicated the king at Torwood in September and was executed the following year. The dictionary records the declaration, states the one point in it that is certainly true, and names the one that is not.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a declaration as a public avowal; to disown as to refuse to acknowledge; a usurper as one who seizes power without right; allegiance as the obligation of a subject; and supremacy as the state of being highest in authority.

expand to see more

DECLARATION, n. An affirmation; a public avowal or proclamation; a publishing or making known.

DISOWN, v.t. To deny; not to own; to refuse to acknowledge as belonging to one's self.

USURPER, n. One who seizes or occupies the power or property of another without right.

ALLEGIANCE, n. The tie or obligation of a subject to his prince or government; loyalty.

SUPREMACY, n. State of being supreme or in the highest station of power; highest authority or power.

Modern Corruption

Nithsdale burgh at whose market cross Richard Cameron and about twenty men read and affixed a declaration disowning Charles II on 22 June 1680, a month before Cameron was killed at Airds Moss.

expand to see more

The dictionary states first the point the Sanquhar men had right, because it is the point the whole quarrel turned on. Charles II had taken to himself a supremacy over the church of Christ, imposing ministers, forbidding assemblies, and requiring oaths acknowledging his headship; that claim is false, and no subject owes obedience to it. The apostolic answer to a magistrate commanding in the things of God is not negotiable: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). The three in Babylon give the form of the refusal, telling a king to his face “that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up” (Dan 3:18), and offering nothing further.

The corruption to name is the step beyond that, and the dictionary names it against men it honours. The Sanquhar Declaration did not merely refuse an unlawful command; it disowned the king's civil authority altogether and declared war. That is a different act, and Scripture does not authorise it. Paul wrote under Nero, whose claims and cruelties exceeded anything the Stuarts attempted, and he wrote “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God” (Rom 13:1). Solomon forbids the political combination by its plainest name, “fear thou the LORD and the king: and meddle not with them that are given to change” (Pro 24:21). Twenty men at a market cross declaring war on a kingdom achieved the death of Cameron within a month, of Cargill within a year, and of Renwick in 1688, and furnished the government with the pretext for the Killing Times. The dictionary holds that refusal unto blood was the course, and that the sword at the cross was a sin which the courage of the men who drew it does not convert into a virtue.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek exousia (G1849), authority; Greek peitharcheo (G3980), to obey authority; Hebrew shanah (H8138), to change.

expand to see more

Greek exousia (G1849) — authority, power, jurisdiction; “there is no power but of God”, Romans 13:1.

Greek hupotasso (G5293) — to subject, to put in subjection; “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers”, Romans 13:1.

Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority; “We ought to obey God rather than men”, Acts 5:29.

Hebrew pelach-sense of serving in the Aramaic of Daniel 3 — “that we will not serve thy gods”, Daniel 3:18.

Hebrew shanah (H8138) — to change, to alter; “them that are given to change”, Proverbs 24:21.

Usage

"“We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — the point the Sanquhar men had right."

"“Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1) — written under Nero."

"“meddle not with them that are given to change” (Pro 24:21) — twenty men declaring war on a kingdom."
